nodes.title: Census identity X^{q^l}-X = prod_{k|l} P_k and existence of degree-l extensions
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with |F| = q = p^w. For k >= 1 let P_k be the product of all monic irreducible polynomials of degree k in F[X], and Pi_F(l) their number. Then for every l >= 1 one has X^{q^l} - X = prod_{k | l} P_k in F[X], hence q^l = sum_{k | l} k Pi_F(k); consequently Pi_F(l) > 0 and there exists an extension field E/F of degree exactly l, necessarily of cardinality q^l and of the form F[X]/(f) for f monic irreducible of degree l.
hypotheses: F finite, so |F| = p^w with p = char F prime (Shoup Thm 7.7), and Z_p is embedded in F
l a positive integer; the identity is an identity of monic polynomials in F[X], not merely of root sets
The squarefreeness step uses the formal derivative D over F and the criterion gcd(f, D(f)) = 1 (Shoup Thm 19.1), which requires D(X^{q^l} - X) = -1, i.e. it uses char F = p | q
proofSteps: Step 1 (squarefreeness): D(X^{q^l}-X) = q^l X^{q^l-1} - 1 = -1 in F[X], so gcd(X^{q^l}-X, D(.)) = 1 and Thm 19.1 gives that X^{q^l}-X is square-free (Shoup p. 513).

Step 2 (divisibility criteria): Thm 19.2 (X^k-1 | X^l-1 in F[X] iff k|l, by division with remainder l = kq+r), Thm 19.3 (a^k-1 | a^l-1 iff k|l for integers a >= 2), and their combination Thm 19.4 (X^{a^k}-X | X^{a^l}-X iff k|l) (Shoup pp. 509-510).

Step 3 (Frobenius criterion): for f monic irreducible of degree k set E := F[X]/(f) = F[xi]. Then f | X^{q^l}-X iff sigma^l(xi) = xi iff sigma^l = id_E iff k | l, using Thm 19.9 (sigma^i = sigma^j iff i == j mod deg) and Thm 16.7 (an F-algebra map is determined on F[xi] by its value at xi) (Shoup p. 513).
Step 4: combining Steps 1-3 gives Thm 19.10; equating degrees gives q^l = sum_{k|l} k Pi_F(k) (Thm 19.11, Shoup p. 514).

Step 5 (existence): the source deduces Pi_F(l) > 0 from Theorem 19.11 ('it is easy to deduce'), and proves it quantitatively as Theorem 19.12: q^l/(2l) <= Pi_F(l) <= q^l/l and Pi_F(l) = q^l/l + O(q^{l/2}/l) (printed p. 514). The extension is then F[X]/(f) for f monic irreducible of degree l. Conversely every degree-l extension E has E = F[gamma] for gamma a generator of the cyclic group E^* (Shoup Thm 7.29), so E is F-algebra isomorphic to F[X]/(phi) with phi the minimal polynomial of gamma (printed p. 511).
acceptance: Check l = 1: X^q - X = prod_{a in F}(X - a) (Shoup Thm 19.6) recovers P_1 and Pi_F(1) = q.
Check that the identity is asserted in F[X] with multiplicities, so that degree comparison is legitimate; a set-theoretic 'same roots' statement is not enough.
Check the degenerate reading: the census identity forces Pi_F(l) > 0 only after the square-freeness step; without it the degree count fails.

nodes.title: The q-power Frobenius: F-algebra automorphism, fixed field, and exact order l
nodes.statement: Let F be finite with |F| = q and let E be an F-algebra. The map sigma: E -> E, sigma(alpha) = alpha^q, is an F-algebra homomorphism; if E is a finite extension field of F then sigma is an F-algebra automorphism whose fixed set is exactly F, and if (E:F) = l then for all i, j in Z one has sigma^i = sigma^j if and only if i == j (mod l). In particular sigma generates a cyclic group of order exactly l and every power of sigma is sigma^i for a unique i in {0,...,l-1}.
hypotheses: q = p^w with p = char F; sigma = tau^w where tau(alpha) = alpha^p, and tau is a ring homomorphism only because char = p
For the automorphism statement E must be a field (injectivity of a ring map between fields) and finite (surjectivity from injectivity)
The fixed-set statement 'sigma(alpha) = alpha iff alpha in F' uses that X^q - X already has its q roots in F
proofSteps: Thm 19.7: E either trivial or contains an isomorphic copy of F, forcing char E = p; then sigma = tau^w is a ring homomorphism, and sigma(c 1_E) = c^q 1_E = c 1_E for c in F by Thm 19.5 (a^q = a for a in F), so sigma is F-algebra (Shoup p. 512).

Thm 19.8: injective since a ring map from a field to a field is injective; surjective by finiteness; fixed points are roots of X^q - X, and all q elements of F are already roots, so by Thm 7.14 there are no others (Shoup p. 512).

Thm 19.9: sigma^i = sigma^j iff sigma^{i-j} = id iff prod_{alpha in E}(X-alpha) | X^{q^{i-j}} - X iff X^{q^l} - X | X^{q^{i-j}} - X (Thm 19.6 applied to E) iff l | (i-j) (Thm 19.4) (Shoup pp. 512-513).
acceptance: Absolute vs relative exponent: for |F| = q = p^w and E of degree l over F, the relative Frobenius sigma is the q-power map and has exact order l on E (Thm 19.9), while the absolute Frobenius tau is the p-power map, with sigma = tau^w (Thm 19.7), and has order wl on E. Record both exponents separately. [Corrected in review: the draft's example ('for F = F_p and E = F_{p^w}, the relative Frobenius over F_q = F_{p^w} is the p^w-power map, and its order over F is l') mixed the base fields and was self-inconsistent.]

Fixed-field test: sigma(alpha) = alpha iff alpha is in F (Thm 19.8), whereas tau(alpha) = alpha iff alpha is in the prime field Z_p. When F != Z_p, any alpha in F outside Z_p is fixed by sigma but not by tau; this distinguishes the two fixed fields. [Corrected in review: the draft said an element fixed by sigma but outside the prime field is 'impossible by Thm 19.8', which holds only when F is the prime field.]

nodes.title: Subfield lattice sigma^k <-> k | l and uniqueness of finite fields up to F-algebra isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let E be an extension of degree l over the finite field F with |F| = q, and sigma the Frobenius of E over F. The intermediate fields K with F subset K subset E are in bijection with the positive divisors k of l, the divisor k corresponding to the subalgebra E^{sigma^k} = {alpha : alpha^{q^k} = alpha}, which has degree k over F. Moreover any two extensions E, E' of the same degree l over F are isomorphic as F-algebras.
hypotheses: E/F finite of degree l; K ranges over intermediate fields, and each such K is automatically the fixed subalgebra of a power of sigma (Thm 19.8 applied with K in place of F)
Uniqueness is uniqueness as F-algebras, i.e. via an isomorphism restricting to the identity on F; it is proved by embedding, not by a cardinality argument alone
proofSteps: Forward direction: for k | l the polynomial X^{q^k}-X divides X^{q^l}-X (Thm 19.4) and X^{q^l}-X splits into distinct monic linear factors over E (Thm 19.6 applied to E), so E^{sigma^k} has exactly q^k elements (Shoup p. 515).
Backward direction: if K is intermediate of degree k then k | l by multiplicativity of degrees and K = E^{sigma^k} by Thm 19.8 applied with K in place of F.

Uniqueness: write E' = F[alpha'], let phi be the minimal polynomial of alpha' (irreducible of degree l). By Thm 19.10 phi | X^{q^l}-X, and by Thm 19.6 applied to E that polynomial splits over E, so phi has a root alpha in E; then F[alpha] is F-isomorphic to F[X]/(phi) and has degree l, hence equals E (Shoup pp. 515-516).
acceptance: The F-algebra isomorphism E -> E' constructed here is a bijection, so the inverse map exists; an implementation must carry the inverse as data rather than assert existence.
Test l = 6: the intermediate fields are exactly those of degrees 1, 2, 3, 6; there is no intermediate field of degree 4 even though 4 <= 6.

Then the intermediate fields K, with F subset-or-equal K subset-or-equal E, are in one-to-one correspondence with the divisors k of l, where the divisor k corresponds to the subalgebra of E fixed by sigma^k, which has degree k over F.

nodes.title: Conjugates, characteristic polynomial, and surjectivity of norm and trace
nodes.statement: Let F be finite of cardinality q, E/F of degree l, sigma the Frobenius. For alpha in E of degree k over F with minimal polynomial phi, k is the least positive integer with sigma^k(alpha) = alpha, the distinct conjugates are alpha, sigma(alpha), ..., sigma^{k-1}(alpha), and phi = prod_{i<k}(X - sigma^i(alpha)); the characteristic polynomial chi := prod_{i<l}(X - sigma^i(alpha)) equals phi^{l/k} and lies in F[X]. Setting N_{E/F}(alpha) = prod_{i<l} sigma^i(alpha) and Tr_{E/F}(alpha) = sum_{i<l} sigma^i(alpha), the norm restricted to E^* is a group homomorphism from E^* onto F^*, and the trace is an F-linear map from E onto F.
hypotheses: E/F finite of degree l over a finite field; both maps take values in F because they are sigma-fixed, equivalently they occur as coefficients of chi up to sign
Surjectivity of N uses that E^* is cyclic of order q^l - 1 and that N(alpha) = alpha^{(q^l-1)/(q-1)}
Surjectivity of Tr uses that the kernel is contained in the root set of X + X^q + ... + X^{q^{l-1}}, of degree q^{l-1} < q^l
proofSteps: Conjugacy: the 'conjugate to' relation is an equivalence relation; minimality of k and injectivity of sigma give i = 0 in sigma^k(alpha) = sigma^i(alpha), whence Thm 19.15 (Shoup pp. 516-517).

Norm: N(alpha) = alpha^{sum_{i<l} q^i} = alpha^{(q^l-1)/(q-1)}; the image of that power map on the cyclic group E^* is the unique subgroup of order q-1 (Thm 6.32), which is F^* (Thm 19.17, Shoup p. 519).

Trace: F-linearity from F-linearity of sigma; the image is an F-subspace of F, hence {0} or F; it is not {0} since the kernel lies in the root set of a polynomial of degree q^{l-1} while |E| = q^l (Thm 19.18, Shoup p. 519).
Degree of alpha via multiplicative order: if alpha in E^* has order r, its degree over F is the multiplicative order of q modulo r (Thm 19.16, Shoup p. 518).
acceptance: Trace target: check that Tr_{E/F} lands in F and is surjective onto F (not merely nonzero); this is the normalization used by additive characters psi = psi_0 o Tr in FF.1.
Norm target: check surjectivity onto F^*, not onto F; N(0) = 0 is treated separately.
Check chi = phi^{l/k} on an element of proper subfield degree, e.g. alpha in F with l > 1, where chi = (X-alpha)^l.

nodes.title: The sheaves L(chi, f_0) attached to a character and a morphism to a commutative algebraic group
nodes.statement: Let G_0 be a connected commutative algebraic group over F_q, L the Lang torsor under the finite group G_0(F_q) defined by the Lang isogeny L(x) = F(x) x^{-1} (exact sequence 0 -> G_0(F_q) -> G_0 -> G_0 -> 0), f_0 : X_0 -> G_0 a morphism from a separated F_q-scheme of finite type, and chi : G_0(F_q) -> E_lambda^* a character into a finite extension E_lambda of Q_l (l != p). Set L(chi, f_0) := chi^{-1}(f_0^* L). This is a lisse E_lambda-sheaf of rank one on X_0 with: (1.7.1)-(1.7.2) bimultiplicativity in chi and in f_0; (1.7.3) compatibility with pullback along g_0 : Y_0 -> X_0; (1.7.4) L(chi, u_0 f_0) = L(chi u_0, f_0) for a homomorphism u_0 : G_0 -> H_0; (1.7.5) the product decomposition for G_0 a product; (1.7.6) F_x^* acts on the stalk at a rational point x by the scalar chi(f_0(x)); and (1.7.7) L(chi, f_0)_1 = L(chi o N_{F_{q^n}/F_q}, f_1) after base change to F_{q^n}.
hypotheses: G_0 connected commutative over F_q (the appendix 1.23-1.26 handles the non-commutative case separately and changes the conclusion: y and y' need not be conjugate)
l != p and E_lambda a finite extension of Q_l; the E_lambda-sheaf formalism of [Rapport] paragraph 2, especially 2.11, is used
The inverse chi^{-1} in the definition is what makes (1.7.6) read F_x^* = chi(f_0(x)) rather than its inverse
X_0 separated of finite type over F_q for the trace formula application in Scholie 1.9
proofSteps: The Lang isogeny L : G_0 -> G_0, x |-> F(x) x^{-1}, is etale with image an open subgroup of the connected G_0, hence all of G_0, and kernel the finite group G_0(F_q); this defines the G_0(F_q)-torsor L (1.4, 1.4.1), with the two model cases G_a (x^q - x) and G_m (x^{q-1}) at (1.4.2), (1.4.3).
1.5 computes the Frobenius on the fibre of the Lang torsor at y in G_0(F_q): on L_y = L^{-1}(y), F* is g |-> g y^{-1}; this is the source of (1.7.6).

1.2 turns a torsor T under a finite abelian A together with a character rho : A -> E_lambda^* into a rank-one lisse sheaf rho(T) with a nowhere-vanishing map p : T -> rho(T) satisfying p(ta) = rho(a) p(t) (1.2.3).

1.3 records that a torsor obtained from an extension of commutative group schemes is additive in the morphism, (f+g)^* T = f^* T + g^* T (1.3.1); with 1.2 this yields the bimultiplicativity (1.7.1)-(1.7.5).
1.6 compares the Lang torsors over F_q and over F_{q^n}: N L(q^n) = L(q) (1.6.2), by identifying prod_i F^{(q^i)} on G_0(F_{q^n}) with the norm followed by the inclusion; this gives (1.7.7).
Combining (1.7.6) with the trace formula (1.1.1) gives Scholie 1.9: sum over s in S_0(F_q) of chi f_0(s) = Tr(F^*, H_c^*(S, L(chi,f_0))), and (1.9.2) over F_{q^n} with chi o N.
acceptance: Take G_0 = {e}: Scholie 1.9 degenerates to |S_0(F_q)| = Tr(F^*, H_c^*(S, E_lambda)) (Remarque 1.9.4); check the construction reproduces the constant sheaf.
Take G_0 = G_a and chi = psi: the sheaf is the Artin-Schreier sheaf; take G_0 = G_m and chi a multiplicative character: the Kummer sheaf. Check (1.7.6) on each.
Check that (1.7.7) is a norm compatibility, not a naive base change: over F_{q^n} the character is chi o N_{F_{q^n}/F_q}, so a stage that forgets the norm produces the wrong Frobenius trace.

nodes.title: Gauss sums as the Frobenius eigenvalue on a one-dimensional H^1_c over G_m
nodes.statement: Let k be a finite field of characteristic p with q elements, chi a character of k^* and psi a non-trivial character of the additive group of k, both with values in E_lambda^*. Define the Gauss sum by tau(chi,psi) = - sum_{x in k^*} psi(x) chi^{-1}(x) (note the sign). Then -tau(chi,psi) = Tr(F^*, H_c^*(G_m, L(psi chi^{-1}))), and the cohomology of G_m with coefficients in L(psi chi^{-1}) satisfies: (i) H_c^i = 0 for i != 1 and dim H_c^1 = 1; (ii) F^* acting on H^1 is multiplication by tau(chi,psi); (iii) if chi is non-trivial then H_c^1 -> H^1 is an isomorphism.
hypotheses: k finite of characteristic p, |k| = q; psi non-trivial additive character (otherwise L(psi) is trivial and the Swan conductor computation fails)
chi any multiplicative character for (i)-(ii); chi non-trivial is required for (iii)
Characters take values in E_lambda^* with l != p, not in C; the passage to complex values is by a choice of embedding
L(psi chi^{-1}) is L(psi) tensor chi(K_{q-1}) where K_n is the Kummer torsor of the exact sequence 0 -> mu_n -> G_m -> G_m -> 0, and on G_m over k the Lang torsor is K_{q-1}
proofSteps: Regard -tau(chi,psi) as a sum over the rational points of G_m and apply Scholie 1.9 with G_0 = G_a x G_m (Sommes trig. 4.1).
Reduce (i)-(iii) to the geometric statement Proposition 4.3 for L(psi) tensor chi(K_n) over G_m/F-bar.

Ramification input: L(psi) is the restriction to G_m of a locally constant sheaf on G_a, wildly ramified at infinity with Swan conductor 1; chi(K_n) is constant if chi = 1, and for chi != 1 it is ramified at 0 and tame there.

Hence L(psi) tensor chi(K_n) is ramified at infinity; by 1.18 b), c) the groups H_c^i vanish for i != 1; and for chi != 1 ramification at both 0 and infinity gives (ii) of Prop. 4.3 via Exemple 1.19.1 (no local monodromy invariants implies R^i j_* = 0 for i > 0, so H_c^* -> H^* is an isomorphism).

Euler characteristic: the Swan conductors are 0 at 0 and 1 at infinity, so by (3.2.1) chi_c = rk . chi(G_m) - sum Sw = 1 . 0 - 1 = -1; with the vanishing in degrees != 1 this forces dim H_c^1 = 1 (Prop. 4.3 end of proof).
With dim H_c^1 = 1, the trace formula identity of step 1 identifies the single Frobenius eigenvalue with tau(chi,psi).
acceptance: Degenerate case psi = 1: L(psi) is trivial, the Swan conductor at infinity is 0, chi_c(G_m) = 0, and the conclusion dim H_c^1 = 1 fails. Test that the construction refuses psi = 1.
Degenerate case chi = 1: (iii) is not asserted; H_c^1 -> H^1 need not be an isomorphism, so the duality argument of Remarque 4.4 is unavailable.
Numerical check: for k = F_p, chi the Legendre symbol and psi(x) = e(x/p), the classical quadratic Gauss sum has absolute value p^{1/2}, matching the eigenvalue statement.

nodes.title: |tau(chi,psi)| = q^{1/2} from Poincare duality on G_m
nodes.statement: If chi is non-trivial then H_c^1(G_m, L(psi chi^{-1})) and H_c^1(G_m, L(psi^{-1} chi)) are in perfect duality with values in E_lambda(-1); consequently tau(chi,psi) . tau(chi^{-1}, psi^{-1}) = q and |tau(chi,psi)| = q^{1/2}.
hypotheses: chi non-trivial (so that 4.2 (iii) H_c^1 -> H^1 is an isomorphism and the duality pairs H_c^1 against H_c^1 rather than against H^1)
psi non-trivial

The duality is Poincare duality on the smooth curve G_m with a Tate twist (-1); the absolute value statement is the statement about complex conjugates of the eigenvalue after an embedding E_lambda -> C
proofSteps: By 4.2 (iii) for chi != 1 the natural map H_c^1 -> H^1 is an isomorphism, so Poincare duality (1.18 c): H^i_c(X,F) and H^{2n-i}(X, F^dual)(2n) are dual for X smooth purely n-dimensional and F lisse) becomes a perfect pairing between the two one-dimensional spaces.
The Frobenius eigenvalues on the two lines are tau(chi,psi) and tau(chi^{-1},psi^{-1}), and the twist (-1) contributes the factor q, giving the product formula.
Taking absolute values of both sides after an embedding into C, and using that the two Gauss sums are complex conjugates, yields |tau(chi,psi)| = q^{1/2}.
acceptance: Degenerate check: chi trivial gives the classical value tau(1,psi) = 1 (sum of psi over k^* equals -1 up to the sign convention), of absolute value 1, not q^{1/2}; the theorem excludes this case.
Check the twist bookkeeping: the factor q comes from E_lambda(-1), so an implementation that drops the Tate twist gets |tau| = 1.
Cross-check against the classical Gauss-sum modulus computation over prime fields.

nodes.title: Gauss sums over an etale F_q-algebra and the sign e(k); Hasse-Davenport as a twisted form
nodes.statement: Let k be an etale algebra over F_q of degree N, a product of fields k_i of degrees N_i, and set e(k) = (-1)^{sum_i (N_i + 1)}, the signature of the permutation of S = Hom_{F_q}(k, F-bar) induced by Frobenius. For psi : F_q -> E_lambda^* non-trivial and chi : k^* -> E_lambda^*, define tau_{F_q}(chi,psi) = (-1)^N sum_{x in k^*} psi(Tr_{k/F_q}(x)) chi^{-1}(x). Then tau_{F_q}(chi,psi) = e(k) prod_i tau(chi_i, psi o Tr_{k_i/F_q}), and the source will interpret the Hasse-Davenport identity (in 4.12) as a twisted form of the following special case of (4.5.3): for the SPLIT algebra k = F_q^N (N copies of F_q, so e(k) = 1) and chi a character of F_q^*, tau_{F_q}(chi o N_{k/F_q}, psi) = tau(chi,psi)^N. The field F_{q^N} is a twisted form of the split algebra F_q^N. [Corrected in review from a page render of volume p. 198: the draft stated the special case for the field k = F_{q^N} with chi a character of F_{q^N}^*, for which chi o N_{k/F_q} is not even defined.]
hypotheses: k etale over F_q of degree N; the decomposition into fields k_i is the one used to define e(k), so the sign depends on the decomposition type, not only on N
psi non-trivial on F_q; chi is a character of the unit group k^*, with coordinates chi_i
The identity (4.5.3) is called 'trivial' in the source; the Hasse-Davenport content is in the twisted-form statement of 4.12, whose proof was not read for this packet
proofSteps: 4.5 defines e(k) as the signature of the Frobenius permutation of the N geometric points of Spec k, equal to (-1)^{sum (N_i+1)}.
Definition (4.5.2) inserts the factor (-1)^N so that (4.5.3) holds with e(k) as stated.

The source announces (Sommes trig. 4.5, end, volume p. 198) that the Hasse-Davenport relation will be interpreted in 4.12 as a twisted form (cf. 1.12) of the special case k = F_q^N (split), chi a character of F_q^*: tau_{F_q}(chi o N_{k/F_q}, psi) = tau(chi,psi)^N, which follows at once from (4.5.3) because chi o N has all coordinates equal to chi and e(k) = 1.
acceptance: Check the sign: for k = F_q^N (split etale algebra, all N_i = 1) one gets e(k) = (-1)^{2N} = 1, while for k = F_{q^N} a field one gets e(k) = (-1)^{N+1}.
Check that the Hasse-Davenport statement involves chi o N and not chi restricted; the norm is the same normalization as in (1.7.7).

nodes.title: The modified pole order v*_x(f) and invariance of the Artin-Schreier sum under f -> f + g^p - g
nodes.statement: Let X_0 be a projective smooth absolutely irreducible curve of genus g over F_q, f a rational function on X_0 (a morphism X_0 -> P^1 not identically infinity), and psi the character x |-> exp(2 pi i Tr_{F_q/F_p}(x) / p). For a closed point x of X_0 put v_x(f) = order of the pole of f at x (0 if f(x) != infinity) and v*_x(f) = inf_g v_x(f + g^p - g). Define S_f = sum' psi(f(x)) over x in X_0(F_q) with v*_x(f) = 0, where psi(f(x)) means psi((f + g^p - g)(x)) for any g with f + g^p - g regular at x. Then S_f = S_{f + g^p - g} for all rational g.
hypotheses: X_0 projective, smooth and absolutely irreducible over F_q; f rational and not identically infinity
The sum is over rational points at which the modified pole order vanishes, not over all points where f is regular; that is the whole point of the normalization
The value psi(f(x)) at such a point is well defined because psi kills the image of the Artin-Schreier operator
proofSteps: Sommes trig. Exemple 3.5 a) defines v_x(f) and v*_x(f) = inf over g of v_x(f + g^p - g).
b) defines psi(f(x)) at a point with v*_x(f) = 0 using any g making f + g^p - g regular at x.
(3.5.1) defines S_f as the sum over the points with v*_x(f) = 0, and the source then states 'On a S_f = S_{f+g^p-g}'.

At the sheaf level the invariance is 1.3: a morphism to G_a that factors through the Artin-Schreier isogeny gives a trivial torsor, so L(psi f) and L(psi (f + g^p - g)) are isomorphic on the open set where f and g are both regular.
acceptance: Check that removing the modification (summing over all x with f(x) != infinity) breaks the invariance: the excluded point set changes under f -> f + g^p - g.
Check the well-definedness of psi(f(x)) by comparing two choices of g.
Check the p = 2 case, where g^p - g = g^2 + g.

nodes.title: Weil's square-root bound for one-variable Artin-Schreier sums on a curve, with conductor-dependent constant
nodes.statement: With X_0, f, psi and S_f as above, assume f is not of the form g^p - g + constant. Then H^i(X-bar, j_* L(psi f)) = 0 for i != 1, S_f = -Tr(F^*, H^1(X-bar, j_* L(psi f))), this H^1 has dimension 2g - 2 + sum_{v*_x(f) > 0} [k(x) : F_q](1 + v*_x(f)), and every complex conjugate of every eigenvalue of F^* on it has absolute value q^{1/2}. Hence |S_f| <= (2g - 2 + sum_{v*_x(f) != 0} [k(x):F_q](1 + v*_x(f))) q^{1/2}.
hypotheses: X_0 projective smooth absolutely irreducible of genus g over F_q; f rational, not identically infinity, and NOT of the form g^p - g + constant
psi non-trivial; the l-adic realization replaces psi by psi_0 o Tr_{F_q/F_p} with psi_0 : F_p -> E_lambda^*, so the coefficients are E_lambda and l != p

j : U_0 -> X_0 is the inclusion of the open set where f is regular ('l'ouvert ou f != infinity'). At points with v_x(f) > 0 but v*_x(f) = 0, j_* L(psi f) is still lisse, because L(psi f) = L(psi(f + g^p - g)) near x (1.3). [Corrected in review: the draft defined U_0 by the normalized condition v*_x(f) = 0.]
The dimension formula requires the Swan conductor computation Sw_x(L(psi f)) = v*_x(f), imported from Serre 1961
The absolute-value statement is for all complex conjugates of the eigenvalues, not for one chosen embedding
proofSteps: Passage from complex to l-adic coefficients: replace psi by psi_0 o Tr with psi_0 : F_p -> E_lambda^*; then (3.5.3) S_f = sum (-1)^i Tr(F^*, H^i(X-bar, j_* L(psi f))).

Local analysis via the trace formula: at a rational point with v*_x(f) = 0 the Frobenius acts on j_*(L(psi f)) by psi(f(x)) (this is 1.7.6 after replacing f by f + g^p - g, which does not change L(psi f) by 1.3); at a point with v*_x(f) != 0 the sheaf is ramified and (j_* L(psi f))_x = 0.

Swan conductor: Sw_x(L(psi f)) = v*_x(f), after reduction to the case v_x(f) = v*_x(f) (so p does not divide v_x(f)) and extension of scalars; Deligne cites J.-P. Serre, 'Sur les corps locaux a corps residuel algebriquement clos', Bull. SMF 89 (1961), pp. 105-154, no. 4.4.

Non-triviality: since psi_0 is injective, triviality of L(psi f) = L(psi_0 f) is equivalent to triviality of the F_p-torsor T^p - T - f = 0 on U; if that torsor were trivial it would be pulled back from an F_p-torsor T^p - T - lambda = 0 on Spec F_q, so f would be of the form g^p - g + lambda. Hence under the stated hypothesis L(psi f) is geometrically non-constant.

Vanishing in degrees != 1: by 1.18 b) (for S connected, F lisse of rank one and non-constant, H_c^0 = 0) together with duality for the top degree; Deligne concludes 'Les H^i(X-bar, j_* L(psi f)) sont donc nuls pour i != 1', so (3.5.3) reduces to (3.5.5) S_f = -Tr(F^*, H^1).

Dimension: by the Euler-Poincare formula (3.2.1) chi_c(F) = rk(F) . chi(X) - sum_{s in S} Sw_s(F) with chi(X) = 2 - 2g - #S, combined with the Swan computation, giving dim H^1 = 2g - 2 + sum_{v*_x(f) > 0} [k(x):F_q](1 + v*_x(f)).

Weights: 3.4 states that when F_0 becomes trivial on a finite covering of X_0, Weil proved that the complex conjugates of the eigenvalues of F^* on H^i(X-bar, j_* F) have absolute value q^{i/2}; L(psi f) becomes trivial on the Artin-Schreier covering, so each of the dim H^1 eigenvalues has absolute value q^{1/2}, and the triangle inequality gives (3.5.2).
acceptance: Degenerate test 1: f = g^p - g + c. Then S_f = psi(c) . #{x : v*_x(f) = 0} is of size about q, while the right-hand side of (3.5.2) can be 2g-2 < q^{1/2}; the hypothesis is therefore not removable.

Degenerate test 2: X_0 = P^1, f a polynomial of degree d with p not dividing d. Then the only pole is at infinity with v*_infinity(f) = d, g = 0, and (3.5.2) gives |sum psi(f(x))| <= (d-1) q^{1/2}, the classical Weil bound.

Check that H^0 and H^2 are not assumed to vanish: their vanishing is derived from geometric non-constancy of the rank-one sheaf (1.18 b)), and a stage that assumes H_c^2 = 0 for a general trace function is unsound.
Check the conductor term: a point with v*_x(f) = 1 of residue degree 1 contributes 2 to the dimension, not 1.

nodes.title: Involution-induced duality: even-dimensional H^1, paired eigenvalues, and the Kloosterman case
nodes.statement: Suppose in addition that there is an automorphism sigma of X_0 with f(sigma x) = -f(x). Then S_f is real; if sigma is involutive, the sheaves F_0 = j_* L(psi f) and G_0 = j_* L(psi(-f)) are in duality, H^1(X-bar, F) carries an alternating perfect pairing with values in E_lambda(1), hence has even dimension, and the eigenvalues of F^* on H^1 are grouped in pairs alpha, q/alpha. For X_0 = P^1, f = x + a/x and sigma x = -x (a != 0) the poles are 0 and infinity with v*_x(f) = 1 at each, so dim H^1 = -2 + 2 + 2 = 2 and sum_{xy=a, x,y in F_{q^n}} psi(Tr_{F_{q^n}/F_p}(x+y)) = -(alpha^n + beta^n) with alpha beta = q.
hypotheses: sigma an automorphism of X_0 with f o sigma = -f, and involutive for the duality statement
The pairing takes values in E_lambda(1); the alternating property uses that sigma acts trivially on E_lambda(1)
The Kloosterman specialization needs a != 0 and the identification of the two poles with v*(f) = 1
proofSteps: 3.6 a): F_0 and G_0 are in duality; b) sigma^* F_0 -> G_0 and sigma^* G_0 -> F_0 with composite the identity; c) the pairing satisfies psi(f.g) = psi(f).psi(g).
Passing to cohomology, H^1(X-bar,F) and H^1(X-bar,G) are in perfect duality with values in E_lambda(1) and the induced bilinear form sigma-composed-with-the-pairing on H^1(X-bar,F) is alternating.
Hence dim H^1 is even (and separately each non-zero v*_x(f) is odd), and the eigenvalues occur in pairs alpha, q/alpha.

Exemple 3.7 specializes to X_0 = P^1, f = x + a/x, sigma x = -x: the poles are 0 and infinity, each with v*_x(f) = 1, so the dimension formula of the previous node gives -2 + 2 + 2 = 2, and the trace identity gives the Kloosterman sum as -(alpha^n + beta^n) with alpha beta = q. Deligne attributes the resulting formula to L. Carlitz, Acta Arith. 16 (1969/70), pp. 179-193.
acceptance: Check the dimension arithmetic 2g - 2 + sum = -2 + (1+1) + (1+1) = 2 for the Kloosterman sheaf on P^1.
Check |Kl(a; q^n)| <= 2 q^{n/2} follows from alpha beta = q together with |alpha| = |beta| = q^{1/2}.

Check p = 2 separately: there -f = f, so the hypothesis reads f o sigma = f (satisfied for instance by sigma = id) rather than being vacuous. The source does not treat p = 2 separately, so the alternating-form argument should be re-checked in that case. [Corrected in review: the draft called the hypothesis vacuous for p = 2.]

nodes.title: Deligne's elementary n-variable bound (d-1) q^{n-1/2} by fibering and the Lang-Weil hyperplane lemma
nodes.statement: Let P in F_q[X_1,...,X_n] be of degree d, not of the form Q^p - Q + constant, and psi(x) = exp(2 pi i Tr_{F_q/F_p}(x)/p). Then |sum_{x_i in F_q} psi(P(x_1,...,x_n))| <= (d-1) q^{n - 1/2}. The auxiliary lemma used is: a hypersurface of degree d in P^r (r >= 1) can pass through all F_q-rational points only if d >= q+1.
hypotheses: P of total degree d; the exclusion P != Q^p - Q + const is required (otherwise the sum is q^n)
The trivial bound q^n makes the statement non-vacuous only when d - 1 < q^{1/2}; the proof assumes only d < q + 1 and treats the rest by the trivial estimate
In Case 2 the reduction P -> P - (P_d - P_d^{1/p}) uses that P_d is a p-th power, so that P_d - P_d^{1/p} = ℘(P_d^{1/p}) lies in the image of the Artin-Schreier operator and the sum is unchanged
proofSteps: Lemme 3.9 is proved by induction on r: if some rational hyperplane is not contained in the hypersurface, apply the inductive hypothesis to the trace of the hypersurface on it; otherwise d is at least the number of rational hyperplanes, which is at least q+1.

Case 1 (p does not divide d): apply Lemme 3.9 to the leading form P_d to find, after a linear change of variables, P_d(1,0,...,0) != 0, i.e. the coefficient of X_1^d is non-zero. A one-variable polynomial of degree d with non-zero leading coefficient and p not dividing d is never of the form Q^p - Q + const, so the one-variable bound (3.5.2) on P^1 gives |sum_{x_1} psi(S(x_1))| <= (d-1) q^{1/2} for each fixed (x_2,...,x_n); summing over the q^{n-1} fibres gives (d-1) q^{n-1/2}.

Case 2 (p divides d, d > 0): if P_d is a p-th power, replace P by P - (P_d - P_d^{1/p}), which does not change the sum and lowers the degree; induct on d. Otherwise the differential of P_d is not identically zero; by Lemme 3.9 arrange after a linear change that it is non-zero at (1,0,...,0), i.e. writing P_d = sum_i X_1^{d-i} S_i(X_2,...,X_n) the linear form S_1 is not identically zero. Normalize S_0 to zero by subtracting an Artin-Schreier term. Let -lambda be the coefficient of X_1^{d-1} in P. For fixed x_2,...,x_n with S_1(x_2,...,x_n) != lambda, the polynomial in X_1 has degree d-1 in its leading behaviour, and the one-variable bound gives |sum_{x_1} psi(P(x_1,x_2,...,x_n))| <= (d-2) q^{1/2}.

Summation (expose p. 28): the exceptional set {S_1(x_2,...,x_n) = lambda} is a hyperplane in F_q^{n-1} with q^{n-2} points. Each of these has inner sum trivially bounded by q, contributing at most q^{n-1}. The remaining q^{n-1} - q^{n-2} points have inner sum at most (d-2) q^{1/2}. The total is < q^{n-1} + (q^{n-1} - q^{n-2})(d-2) q^{1/2} < (d-2) q^{n-1/2} + q^{n-1} < (d-1) q^{n-1/2}. [Corrected in review: the draft said the exceptional locus 'carries at most q^{n-1} tuples estimated trivially by q', which would give q^n.]
acceptance: Degenerate test: P = Q^p - Q gives sum = q^n, violating the conclusion; the exclusion hypothesis is necessary.
Sanity test n = 1: the statement reduces to the classical |sum psi(P(x))| <= (d-1) q^{1/2}.
Check the final arithmetic (d-2) q^{n-1/2} + q^{n-1} < (d-1) q^{n-1/2}, which needs q^{n-1} < q^{n-1/2}, i.e. it uses q > 1 in the stated form of the source's chain of inequalities.

nodes.title: The Euler-Poincare formula with Swan conductors used by the curve estimates (imported, proof not read)
nodes.statement: Let X-bar be a projective smooth connected curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field k, X a dense open complement of a finite set S of points, F a lisse E_lambda-sheaf on X, chi(X) = 2 - 2g - #S, and Sw_s(F) the Swan conductor at s in S. Then chi_c(F) = sum (-1)^i dim H_c^i(X,F) = rk(F) . chi(X) - sum_{s in S} Sw_s(F), and this equals chi(F) = sum (-1)^i dim H^i(X,F).
hypotheses: X-bar projective smooth connected of genus g over an algebraically closed field; X dense open with finite complement S
F lisse on X (not merely constructible); rk(F) is its rank
Sw_s measures wild ramification at s and is an integer
